events-are-evidence-not-little-pictures.idea: A detector gives clues about a particle by recording what happens as it passes.
events-are-evidence-not-little-pictures.explanation: One event is the set of readings from one collision or decay. A detector can record a trail of hits, their times and the energy left behind. Scientists compare these clues with predictions for different particles. Many events help them test the explanation.

example.title: One curved track
steps: In a known magnetic field, the trail of hits from one charged particle bends.
How sharply the trail bends helps estimate the particle’s momentum if its charge is known. The bend alone cannot tell which kind of particle made it.

terms.definition: A set of measurements from one collision or decay.
A directed quantity describing motion and used in conservation laws.
A field that can turn a compass and push sideways on a moving electric charge.

keep-c-in-the-units.idea: Energy, momentum and mass each have their own units.
keep-c-in-the-units.explanation: Particle physicists use the gigaelectronvolt (GeV) for energy. The letter c stands for the speed of light in empty space. Dividing GeV by c gives a unit for momentum. Dividing GeV by c twice gives a unit for mass. Some calculations choose units in which c has the value 1.

example.title: A particle's total energy
steps: Its rest energy is 3 GeV and momentum times c is 4 GeV.
The total energy is √(3² + 4²) = 5 GeV.

terms.definition: One billion electronvolts, an energy unit.
Vacuum light speed.
Mass multiplied by c squared.

antiparticles-reverse-some-labels.idea: An antiparticle has the same mass as its partner but opposite electric charge.
antiparticles-reverse-some-labels.explanation: The electron's antiparticle is the positively charged positron. Antimatter does not have negative mass or negative detected energy. Neutral particles need other labels to establish whether a distinct antiparticle exists.

example.title: An electron and positron
steps: The electron has charge −e and the positron has charge +e.
Both have the same positive rest mass.

terms.definition: A partner with reversed additive quantum charges.
The positive elementary charge.
A property that comes in two signs, positive and negative. Like signs repel and opposite signs attract.

a-resonance-is-short-lived.idea: A short-lived particle can leave a pattern in its decay products instead of a track.
a-resonance-is-short-lived.explanation: A resonance is a temporary state associated with a characteristic energy range. Repeated product combinations may reveal it. Backgrounds and detector blurring can also shape a peak, so a bump alone is insufficient.

example.title: A synthetic five-GeV mass peak
steps: In an invented dataset, many two-particle combinations gather near a mass of 5 GeV/c².
That excess may suggest a short-lived state, but first compare it with known background processes and the instrument's measurement blur.

terms.definition: A short-lived state that can produce a concentration of events around a characteristic energy.
How much the instrument blurs measured values.
A particle-mass unit based on one billion electronvolts of rest energy.

organize-quarks-and-leptons.idea: Quarks and leptons are two different families of matter particles.
organize-quarks-and-leptons.explanation: Quarks carry the strong interaction's color charge; leptons do not. Their generations repeat charge patterns with different masses. A generation is a family label, not a stage in a particle's life.

example.title: Adding proton charge labels
steps: Two up quarks contribute +4e/3 and one down quark contributes −e/3.
The sum is +e, matching the proton's charge.

terms.definition: A matter particle carrying color charge.
A matter particle without color charge.
An internal strong-interaction label, unrelated to visible colour.

interactions-follow-a-gauge-framework.idea: Some mathematical descriptions can change while every physical prediction stays the same.
interactions-follow-a-gauge-framework.explanation: Electric potential can be shifted by the same constant everywhere without changing its differences. Since these differences determine the electric field in a static situation, this change of description leaves predictions unchanged. Gauge freedom generalizes this idea to allowed changes of field descriptions.

example.title: Changing the zero of potential
steps: Two points have electric potentials of 3 V and 8 V, a difference of 5 V.
Add 10 V everywhere: they become 13 V and 18 V, still differing by 5 V, so the static electric-field prediction stays the same.

terms.definition: Allowed changes in mathematical description that leave physical predictions unchanged.
Electric potential energy per unit charge.
A rule for the force per unit positive charge at a place. Its direction is the way a small positive test charge would be pushed.

hadrons-are-composite.idea: A hadron is a composite particle involving quarks and gluons.
hadrons-are-composite.explanation: A simple valence-quark label tracks important charges, but does not list every contribution to the full state. Ordinary baryons use three valence quarks; ordinary mesons use a quark and antiquark.

example.title: The proton's valence label
steps: Its label is uud, with charges +2e/3, +2e/3 and −e/3.
Adding them gives the proton's charge +e.

terms.definition: A composite particle involving the strong interaction.
A compact quark assignment tracking a hadron's main quantum numbers.
A carrier of the strong interaction.

separate-success-from-open-questions.idea: A successful theory can still leave major questions unanswered.
separate-success-from-open-questions.explanation: The Standard Model explains many measured particle processes. Its success does not by itself explain gravity, dark-matter identity or the origin of neutrino masses. An unexplained observation is not proof of one favored extension.

example.title: One synthetic scattering test
steps: A model predicts 100 events with a stated uncertainty of 10; a compatible measurement finds 104.
This agreement supports the tested prediction, but it does not reveal what dark matter is.

terms.definition: The theory describing known matter particles and electromagnetic, weak and strong interactions.
Extra gravitating matter inferred from astronomical observations, whose microscopic identity is not established by this test.
How precisely a measurement or estimate is known. A value written with ± needs an explanation of what its range means.

an-invariant-survives-a-transformation.idea: Invariant mass stays the same when inertial observers assign different energies and momenta.
an-invariant-survives-a-transformation.explanation: Energy and momentum depend on the observer's frame. Their particular combination gives the same mass for the same system. Use measurements from one frame consistently.

example.title: One frame's measurements
steps: Total energy is 5 GeV and momentum times c is 4 GeV.
The rest energy is √(25 − 16) = 3 GeV, giving mass 3 GeV/c².

terms.definition: Unchanged under a specified transformation.
A viewpoint in which an isolated object moves at constant velocity.

continuous-symmetry-links-to-conservatio.idea: Imagine starting the same experiment a little later. If the rules stay exactly the same however much you shift the start time, that tells you something about energy.
continuous-symmetry-links-to-conservatio.explanation: A change that leaves the rules unchanged is a symmetry. For an isolated system with this continuous time symmetry, total energy is conserved. Energy can move between parts of the system while the total stays fixed.

example.title: A battery heats a resistor
steps: A battery supplies 10 joules to a resistor, which gains 10 joules of internal energy in an ideal insulated model.
The resistor's energy rises, but the battery loses the same amount, preserving the total.

terms.definition: The full laws do not depend on which instant is called time zero.
Having an unchanged total for the complete system.
Something you take as true for a calculation, such as assuming that a cart’s speed stays steady.

parity-and-charge-conjugation-differ.idea: Reversing space and swapping particles for antiparticles are different operations.
parity-and-charge-conjugation-differ.explanation: Parity reverses position coordinates. Charge conjugation swaps particle and antiparticle labels. Whether an interaction preserves either symmetry must be tested; an appealing mirror picture does not establish it.

example.title: Apply parity to one position
steps: The coordinate +2 m becomes −2 m.
This does not turn an electron into a positron, because that would be a different operation.

terms.definition: Spatial inversion.
Exchange of particle and antiparticle labels.

internal-labels-are-not-directions-in-th.idea: Changing an internal quantum state need not move anything through the laboratory.
internal-labels-are-not-directions-in-th.explanation: Particles have internal properties as well as positions. A quantum calculation may change one internal state into another while leaving the particle's location unchanged. A matrix is a table of numbers used as the rule for changing the state's components.

example.title: A two-component swap
steps: Apply the swap matrix [[0,1],[1,0]] to the state column (1,0).
The result is (0,1): the internal state changes, without a one-metre movement in space.

terms.definition: A description of properties other than ordinary position.
A table of numbers used to combine or change components.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

conserve-the-whole-four-momentum.idea: Conserve energy and every momentum component together.
conserve-the-whole-four-momentum.explanation: Four-momentum packages these quantities into one relativistic description. Opposite outgoing momenta can cancel, but their positive energies add. Include all participants in the event.

example.title: A parent at rest emits two photons
steps: Equal photon energies require equal momentum magnitudes pointing in opposite directions.
Their energies add to the parent's rest energy while their momenta sum to zero.

terms.definition: The combined relativistic description of energy and three momentum components.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.
One packet of electromagnetic radiation. Visible light and radio waves can both be described in photons.

two-body-decay-fixes-rest-frame-energies.idea: Two-body decay fixes the product energies once the parent and product masses are known.
two-body-decay-fixes-rest-frame-energies.explanation: In the parent's rest frame, the two momenta are equal and opposite. Equal momentum does not always mean equal energy. For two massless products, each receives half the parent's rest energy.

example.title: An 8 GeV parent rest energy
steps: The parent decays into exactly two massless products.
Each has energy 4 GeV and momentum magnitude 4 GeV/c, in opposite directions.

two-body-decay-fixes-rest-frame-energies.equation: E_each = Mc²/2 for two massless products

terms.definition: The frame in which the parent has zero momentum.
The parent mass.

reconstruct-invariant-mass.idea: A group of massless particles can have nonzero total invariant mass.
reconstruct-invariant-mass.explanation: Add their energies and momentum vectors first. The mass of the combined system includes their relative motion energy. It is not simply the sum of individual rest masses.

example.title: Two opposite photons
steps: Each photon has energy 3 GeV, and their momenta cancel.
The pair has energy 6 GeV and invariant mass 6 GeV/c².

terms.definition: The rest-frame energy of the whole system divided by c squared.
A list of components that can be added and scaled together. A familiar example is a displacement arrow with length and direction.
One packet of electromagnetic radiation. Visible light and radio waves can both be described in photons.

compare-collider-and-fixed-target-energy.idea: Opposing beams can put more total energy into the centre-of-mass frame.
compare-collider-and-fixed-target-energy.explanation: A beam striking a stationary target gives the combined system momentum. Some laboratory energy therefore describes motion of the whole system. Equal opposing beams can cancel that momentum.

example.title: One fixed-target example
steps: For equal particle masses with rest energy 1 GeV and beam total energy 7 GeV, E_CM² = 2 + 14.
The centre-of-mass energy is 4 GeV.

terms.definition: The frame where total momentum is zero.
Beam total energy, including rest energy.

lifetime-and-width-are-reciprocal.idea: A shorter-lived isolated resonance has a larger intrinsic energy width.
lifetime-and-width-are-reciprocal.explanation: Use the state's proper mean lifetime: the average wait measured in its rest frame. The width here is the full width at half the ideal peak height. Detector blur is a separate effect.

example.title: A very short lifetime
steps: Use τ = 2 × 10⁻²⁴ s and ħ = 6.582 × 10⁻²⁵ GeV s.
The intrinsic width is about 0.3291 GeV.

terms.definition: Lifetime measured in the particle's rest frame.
Intrinsic energy full width at half maximum.
Planck's constant divided by 2π.

branching-fractions-divide-decay-possibi.idea: A branching fraction tells what share of decays follows one channel.
branching-fractions-divide-decay-possibi.explanation: Each channel contributes part of the total decay rate. Divide its partial width by the total. This share concerns physical decays, not the fraction successfully seen by a detector.

example.title: Two decay channels
steps: Their partial widths are 2 and 3 in the same units, totaling 5.
The first channel's branching fraction is 2/5 = 0.40.

terms.definition: The probability that a decay uses a specified channel.
A channel's contribution to the total decay width.

cross-section-measures-process-likelihoo.idea: A cross section describes the likelihood of a specified process at a specified energy.
cross-section-measures-process-likelihoo.explanation: It is not a fixed geometric size stamped on a particle. Predictions and measurements must count the same final states. Multiply it by collision luminosity to get a rate before detector losses.

example.title: One process rate
steps: Luminosity is 10³⁰ cm⁻²s⁻¹ and cross section is 10⁻³⁰ cm².
The expected process rate is one event per second.

terms.definition: The collision exposure rate used to convert cross section into event rate.
An area-valued measure of process likelihood.

count-expected-events.idea: Expected detected counts combine exposure, process likelihood, decay share and efficiency.
count-expected-events.explanation: First estimate how many parent processes occur. Then apply the fraction entering the chosen decay channel and the fraction detected. The result is an average, not a guaranteed count or discovery claim.

example.title: Four expected signal events
steps: Exposure 10 fb⁻¹ times cross section 2 fb gives 20 parent processes.
Branching fraction 0.25 leaves five channel events, and efficiency 0.8 gives four expected detections.

terms.definition: Collision exposure added over time.
The chosen decay's branching fraction.
Detection efficiency.
A femtobarn, a cross-section area unit.
An effective area that measures how likely a particular interaction is under the stated conditions.

diagrams-organize-amplitudes.idea: A particle diagram helps organize a calculation about a possible outcome. Its lines tell you which contribution to calculate.
diagrams-organize-amplitudes.explanation: Each contribution gives an amplitude, a number that can combine with the others in a way that strengthens or weakens the result. Add amplitudes for the same outcome before calculating its chance. A line inside the diagram represents part of that calculation. A detector records the particles that actually arrive.

example.title: Two toy contributions
steps: The same outcome receives amplitudes +1 and −1.
They sum to zero, so the toy probability is zero rather than 1 + 1.

terms.definition: A signed or complex quantity whose squared magnitude gives a probability in the stated model.

a-small-coupling-supports-an-expansion.idea: A small interaction strength can make stepwise corrections useful.
a-small-coupling-supports-an-expansion.explanation: Start with a leading calculation and add justified corrections. The first result is not exact. Even a small coupling does not guarantee that an expansion works near every threshold or in every regime.

example.title: One correction
steps: The leading prediction is 100 units and the next calculated correction is −3 units.
The updated result is 97 units, with further corrections still uncalculated.

terms.definition: A parameter describing interaction strength.
A calculation organized into successive contributions.

weak-interactions-have-charged-and-neutr.idea: Some weak interactions transfer electric charge between matter particles and some do not.
weak-interactions-have-charged-and-neutr.explanation: The weak interaction has two main kinds of channel. W particles connect changes that transfer electric charge, while Z particles connect neutral-current changes. Charge must still balance across the whole event; neutral current does not mean every participant is neutral.

example.title: A neutrino absorbed by a neutron
steps: An electron neutrino can interact with a neutron to produce a proton and an electron, if enough energy is available.
Initial electric charge is zero; the final +e proton and −e electron still total zero.

terms.definition: Electron neutrino, a neutral particle involved in the electron family's weak interactions.
Neutron.
Proton.
Electron.
A weak channel in which W exchange transfers charge between matter particles.
A weak channel associated with Z exchange.
A property that comes in two signs, positive and negative. Like signs repel and opposite signs attract.

neutrino-flavor-can-oscillate.idea: A neutrino's later flavor measurement can differ from its production flavor.
neutrino-flavor-can-oscillate.explanation: Flavor names the neutrino type produced or detected in an interaction. A flavor is a mixture of states with different masses. As these wave-like components travel, their cycle stages shift relative to one another, changing the chances of detecting each flavor.

example.title: A two-flavor ideal case
steps: Use a two-flavor model with mixing angle 45° and travel phase π/2 radians, a quarter cycle.
Both squared-sine factors are then 1, so this ideal model gives conversion probability 1.

terms.definition: Mixing angle, describing the proportions of the two mass states.
Their accumulated relative cycle shift during travel.
Sine, an angle function; sin(90°) and sin(π/2) are both 1.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

color-neutrality-is-a-quantum-property.idea: Color neutrality is different from having zero electric charge.
color-neutrality-is-a-quantum-property.explanation: Color names an internal strong-interaction property, not visible pigment. A color-singlet state is unchanged by the relevant color transformations. A proton can therefore be electrically charged and color neutral at once.

example.title: One proton
steps: Its electric charge is +e.
Its physical state is nevertheless color neutral, because those labels describe different interactions.

terms.definition: A state unchanged by the relevant color-symmetry transformations.
The positive elementary charge.
A property that comes in two signs, positive and negative. Like signs repel and opposite signs attract.

add-hadron-quantum-numbers.idea: A proton and a neutron have different electric charge, but both have a baryon number of one. These are two different things to count.
add-hadron-quantum-numbers.explanation: Protons and neutrons belong to a family of particles built from quarks, called hadrons. To find baryon number, count each quark as one third and each antiquark as minus one third. Use the particles’ electric charges in a separate sum to find total charge.

example.title: An up–antidown meson
steps: An up quark and a down antiquark have baryon numbers +⅓ and −⅓, adding to zero.
Their electric charges +⅔e and +⅓e instead add to +e, so zero baryon number does not mean zero electric charge.

terms.definition: The quantum-number count defined here from quarks minus antiquarks.
A hadron with a quark-antiquark valence assignment in the ordinary model.
A property that comes in two signs, positive and negative. Like signs repel and opposite signs attract.

strong-coupling-depends-on-scale.idea: Strong-interaction calculations use different tools at short and long distances.
strong-coupling-depends-on-scale.explanation: At high probing momentum, the effective coupling is often smaller, helping stepwise calculations. At long distances, isolated colored particles are not observed. Making hadrons from quarks and gluons needs additional treatment.

example.title: A short-distance collision
steps: A large momentum transfer can make a quark-and-gluon expansion useful.
Predicting the measured hadrons still requires a model of their formation.

terms.definition: An interaction-strength parameter.
A composite particle involving quarks and gluons.

jets-connect-partons-to-measured-hadrons.idea: A jet is a defined group of measured particles, not a bare quark track.
jets-connect-partons-to-measured-hadrons.explanation: A high-energy quark or gluon can develop into many hadrons. A jet algorithm says how to group the measurements. Use the same grouping rule when comparing predictions with data.

example.title: One specified grouping
steps: The rule includes particles of energies 3, 4 and 5 GeV.
Their energies total 12 GeV; their momentum still requires adding directions as well as sizes.

terms.definition: A group of reconstructed particles formed by a specified clustering rule.
A composite strong-interaction particle.

symmetry-restricts-mass-terms.idea: An equation's mass terms must fit the symmetry rules of its fields.
symmetry-restricts-mass-terms.explanation: A theory's equations must keep the same physical meaning under its allowed changes of field description. A proposed mass term must pass this test too. The Higgs mechanism lets some Standard Model masses fit these rules; it does not work by dragging particles slower.

example.title: A toy product that fails a symmetry test
steps: Suppose an allowed change flips field A's sign but leaves field B unchanged.
A proposed term A × B flips sign, so it cannot stand alone in an expression required to stay unchanged; a compatible structure is needed.

terms.definition: A part of a theory's equations that describes particle mass.
A quantity defined across space and time.
An allowed change that preserves the relevant physical rules.

the-higgs-field-and-boson-differ.idea: A Higgs boson is a disturbance in the Higgs field.
the-higgs-field-and-boson-differ.explanation: A field assigns a value to every place. The Higgs field has a background value even in its lowest-energy state. A collision can put energy into the field and create a Higgs boson. When the boson decays into other particles, the background field is still there.

example.title: One Higgs boson decays
steps: Consider a Higgs boson produced in a collision and later detected through a two-photon decay.
The added disturbance has become other particles, while the field's lowest-energy background remains.

terms.definition: One allowed packet of added excitation in a field.
One packet of light energy.

infer-higgs-properties-from-channels.idea: Different observed decay counts need not mean different production physics.
infer-higgs-properties-from-channels.explanation: Each decay channel has its own branching fraction, background and detection efficiency. Account for these before comparing channels. A single excess does not establish every Higgs property.

example.title: One channel from 100 produced bosons
steps: In a synthetic example, 100 bosons are produced and 10% decay through a chosen channel.
If only half of those events are detected, the expected observed count is 5; this does not mean only five bosons were produced.

terms.definition: The fraction of decays following one channel.
The fraction of relevant events successfully detected.

composite-mass-includes-interaction-ener.idea: A composite object's mass includes internal motion and field energy.
composite-mass-includes-interaction-ener.explanation: Its mass equals total energy in its rest frame divided by c squared. It need not equal the sum of constituent masses. Strong-interaction dynamics supply most of an ordinary nucleon's mass.

example.title: One toy bound system
steps: Its rest-frame energy is 10 GeV.
Its mass is 10 GeV/c², even if its constituents' separate rest masses add to less.

terms.definition: Made of interacting constituents.
A proton or neutron.

curvature-measures-transverse-momentum.idea: Track curvature measures momentum perpendicular to a known magnetic field.
curvature-measures-transverse-momentum.explanation: In an ideal magnetic-only field, the direction changes without the field doing work. A larger perpendicular momentum bends less. Charge magnitude and field strength must also be known.

example.title: One charged track
steps: Use charge magnitude e, field 2 T and radius 1 m.
The perpendicular momentum is approximately 0.300 × 2 × 1 = 0.600 GeV/c.

terms.definition: Momentum perpendicular to the magnetic field in this relation.
The magnetic-field unit.
At a right angle, like two sides that meet at the corner of a square.
A field that can turn a compass and push sideways on a moving electric charge.

missing-momentum-is-an-imbalance.idea: Missing transverse momentum is inferred from what the detector did measure.
missing-momentum-is-an-imbalance.explanation: Add visible momentum vectors and reverse the total. Invisible particles can cause an imbalance, but so can missed or mismeasured visible particles. The result is evidence to model, not a unique particle identity.

example.title: One visible imbalance
steps: Visible x-momenta are +5 and −2 GeV/c, with total y-momentum zero.
The missing transverse estimate is (−3,0) GeV/c.

terms.definition: Perpendicular to the beam direction in this event measurement.
A list of components that can be added and scaled together. A familiar example is a displacement arrow with length and direction.

an-excess-needs-a-statistical-comparison.idea: More events than expected do not automatically establish a new signal.
an-excess-needs-a-statistical-comparison.explanation: A background model predicts a range of possible counts. Compare the observation with that distribution and its uncertainties. A p-value concerns outcomes under a specified model, not the probability that the model is true.

example.title: Five extra events
steps: Observe 25 events when background expectation is 20.
The estimated excess is five, but its strength depends on fluctuations and background uncertainty.

terms.definition: Processes other than the proposed signal.
Under the stated model, the probability of an outcome at least as incompatible by the chosen test.
How precisely a measurement or estimate is known. A value written with ± needs an explanation of what its range means.

systematics-can-move-many-measurements-t.idea: A shared calibration error can move many measurements in the same direction.
systematics-can-move-many-measurements-t.explanation: More data can reduce random counting noise without removing a shared offset. Track which uncertainties are linked. Treating them all as independent can give a misleading total uncertainty.

example.title: A one-percent energy-scale shift
steps: Two true line energies of 100 and 200 units are both read 1% too high, as 101 and 202.
Each absolute reading is wrong, but their ratio remains 2 because the same scale factor affects both.

terms.definition: The mapping from instrument response to measured physical values.
Uncertainty that links changes in more than one measurement.
Individual outcomes can vary even when you repeat the same setup.
How precisely a measurement or estimate is known. A value written with ± needs an explanation of what its range means.
One amount divided by another. Three red counters for every two blue gives a red-to-blue ratio of 3/2.

reconstruct-a-synthetic-two-photon-event.idea: Two-photon invariant mass depends on both energies and the angle between them.
reconstruct-a-synthetic-two-photon-event.explanation: Use all measurements in one frame. Opposite directions give a larger pair mass than parallel directions at the same energies. This calculation alone does not identify a real resonance.

example.title: Two opposite photons
steps: The photon energies are 2 and 8 GeV, and their opening angle is π.
The mass squared times c⁴ is 2 × 2 × 8 × 2 = 64 GeV², giving mass 8 GeV/c².

terms.definition: The angle between the two photon directions.
The combined system's rest-frame energy divided by c squared.
One packet of electromagnetic radiation. Visible light and radio waves can both be described in photons.

audit-a-yield-estimate.idea: Check whether a quoted cross section already includes the chosen decay channel.
audit-a-yield-estimate.explanation: If it does, multiplying by its branching fraction again counts the same probability twice. Efficiency may also include several losses. State what each supplied factor already contains.

example.title: An already specified channel
steps: Exposure 50 fb⁻¹ times channel cross section 0.4 fb gives 20 expected channel events.
Efficiency 0.30 leaves six selected events; do not apply the branching fraction again.

terms.definition: The share of decays entering the chosen channel.
Total collision exposure.
Selection efficiency.
An effective area that measures how likely a particular interaction is under the stated conditions.

reject-a-process-for-a-stated-reason.idea: Reject a proposed process by naming the conservation rule it fails.
reject-a-process-for-a-stated-reason.explanation: Check the complete initial and final states. A charge-balanced story still needs energy and momentum checks. Missing participants can make an incomplete account appear impossible.

example.title: An isolated neutral parent
steps: It is proposed to produce two +e particles and nothing else.
Final charge would be +2e instead of zero, so this complete proposal fails charge conservation.

terms.definition: An unchanged total for the full process.
The positive elementary charge.

know-where-the-bridge-ends.idea: A particle-physics claim needs a model, detector prediction and comparison with uncertain data.
know-where-the-bridge-ends.explanation: First predict what a process produces, then predict how the detector records it. Compare that predicted measurement with data and uncertainty. This course links these steps; deriving the interactions themselves needs quantum field theory, the mathematical framework for interacting particle fields.

example.title: A synthetic detector prediction
steps: A model predicts 10 detected events with a supplied uncertainty of 3, and the experiment sees 12.
The values are compatible at this level, but other models may also fit; the agreement does not establish a unique explanation.

terms.definition: A mathematical framework describing quantum fields and their interactions.
Not clearly in disagreement at the stated uncertainty level.
How precisely a measurement or estimate is known. A value written with ± needs an explanation of what its range means.
